title: Why Do the Wicked Do So Well?
overview: Job answers his friends' claim that bad people always suffer by pointing out that, in real life, many of them live long, happy lives and die in peace.

parts.label: Just hear me out (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: Job asks his friends simply to listen, saying that would comfort him more than their speeches, and after that they can go on mocking. His real complaint is with God, not with people, and what he is about to say shakes him so much he trembles.

parts.label: The wicked thrive (vv. 7-16)
parts.note: Job describes people who brush God aside yet grow old and powerful, with safe homes, healthy herds, dancing children and a peaceful death. This directly contradicts his friends' claim that the wicked live in fear and die young, though Job insists he wants no part in their way of thinking.

parts.label: How often do they fall? (vv. 17-21)
parts.note: Job takes his friends' sayings, that the wicked are snuffed out like a lamp or blown away like straw, and asks how often that really happens. He also rejects the idea that God punishes their children instead, since the wicked do not care what happens to their families once they are gone.

parts.label: Death treats everyone alike (vv. 22-26)
parts.note: Job suggests his friends are telling God how the world ought to work instead of looking at how it does. One person dies healthy and comfortable, another dies bitter and deprived, and both end up in the same dust.

parts.label: Ask anyone who travels (vv. 27-30)
parts.note: Job says he knows what his friends mean when they ask where the homes of the great and the wicked have gone; some interpreters think they are quietly pointing at Job's own losses. He tells them to ask travelers, who say the wicked are often spared disaster, though verse 30 can also be read as saying they are kept for a judgment that comes later, and scholars are unsure which is meant.

parts.label: An honored end (vv. 31-34)
parts.note: No one confronts the wicked or pays them back; they are carried to the grave, their tomb is watched over, and they share the same end as the countless people before and after them. So Job calls his friends' comfort empty, because their answers do not fit the facts.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Job is leaving room for justice after death here (reading verse 30 as the wicked being kept for a later judgment) or is honestly saying that, as far as anyone can see, the wicked simply get away with it.
think: When you look at who does well and who suffers in the world around you, does it seem fair, and how do you make sense of the times it doesn't?
